_about: The recommendation framework: how a visitor’s situation and limits turn into one pick. Read by lib/evidence/recommend.ts and rendered on /what-should-i-use. The rules here are the public promise; keep them in plain English. Every otherSide line states a published finding and links to it: no unsourced numbers, no first-person quotes.
promise: Tell us what’s going wrong and what you can live with. We rule out every tool that breaks one of your limits, show you why, and give you one pick and one alternative from what’s left. Your situation decides what’s eligible. It never changes a score.
rules: Diagnose before recommending. The first question is what’s going wrong, because the right tool depends on the problem, not the category someone typed.
No tool is a real answer. When the problem isn’t one a tool fixes, we say so and point to the guidance instead.

Limits rule tools out; they never re-score them. A tool either fits every limit you set or it’s out, with the reason shown. The order among the tools that fit is the public score, the same for everyone.
Unknown is not yes. If we have no dated evidence that a tool meets a limit, it can’t be the pick. It’s listed under couldn’t check.
One pick and one alternative, never a list. The alternative is the best-scoring tool that’s cheaper for your situation; if none is cheaper, the next best score.
Only scored tools can be the pick. Tools too new to score appear as worth watching, labeled.
Show the real cost for your situation: the cheapest way to pay for your timeline, and what it costs if you forget to cancel.
If nothing fits, say so, and show the closest tool and exactly what it would take.
Every answer includes what the other side of the table sees, from published research, with the source.
Commissions never touch the answer. Whether we earn anything from a tool has no input anywhere in this framework.
Same situation, same answer. Every answer has its own link, a date, and can be quoted.

research.title: Why a broken limit is a hard no
research.finding: Elimination by aspects: people choose by picking an attribute that matters, dropping every option that fails it, and repeating until one is left. A strength on one attribute can’t make up for a failure on another.
research.usedFor: Your limits work the same way: a tool that breaks one is out, however good it is at something else.
research.source: Tversky, A. (1972). Elimination by aspects: A theory of choice. Psychological Review, 79, 281-299.

research.title: Why one pick, not ten
research.finding: A meta-analysis of 99 observations found that more options lower satisfaction and confidence when the choice is complex, the decision is hard, preferences are uncertain, and people want to minimize effort.
research.usedFor: A job search or a hiring crunch hits all four, so the answer is one pick and one alternative, never a ranked list of ten.
research.source: Chernev, A., Bockenholt, U., and Goodman, J. (2015). Choice overload: A conceptual review and meta-analysis. Journal of Consumer Psychology, 25(2), 333-358.

problems.label: I apply and hear nothing back
problems.why: Silence usually starts before a person reads anything: an applicant tracking system screens your resume against the posting first. A checker shows you what it sees.

otherSide.line: Hiring teams know their systems screen out good people. In a Harvard Business School and Accenture study, 88% of employers agreed that qualified, high-skilled candidates get screened out for not matching a job description’s exact criteria. Use the posting’s own words.
otherSide.source: Hidden Workers: Untapped Talent, Harvard Business School and Accenture, 2021

problems.label: I need to rebuild my resume
problems.why: A builder gets you a clean, readable layout fast. The words are still yours to get right.

otherSide.line: In Ladders’ 2018 eye-tracking study, a recruiter’s first pass on a resume averaged 7.4 seconds, and the resumes that held attention had simple layouts with clear section headings. Pick the plainest template the builder offers.
otherSide.source: Ladders eye-tracking study, 2018, reported by HR Dive

problems.label: I’m losing track of applications
problems.why: A tracker keeps every application, contact and follow-up in one place, so nothing goes quiet without you noticing.

otherSide.line: Follow-ups count, and almost nobody sends them. In a 2017 Accountemps survey of more than 300 HR managers, 80% said they consider thank-you notes when choosing a candidate, yet they received notes from only 24% of applicants. Track the follow-up, not just the application.
otherSide.source: Accountemps survey of US HR managers, 2017, reported by HR Dive

problems.label: I get interviews, but no offers
problems.why: This one isn’t your resume, so a resume tool won’t fix it. Practice will. None of the practice tools has enough public reviews to score yet.

otherSide.line: Interview performance is coachable. In a study of 144 people taking structured interviews, those given more thorough coaching earned higher interview ratings. Rehearse out loud, with someone scoring your answers.
otherSide.source: Tross, S. A., and Maurer, T. J. (2008). Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology

problems.label: I don’t know what to apply for
problems.why: No tool fixes this one, and anyone selling you one is guessing. Pick the roles first, then come back for the tools.

guidance.text: Start with the job seeker guides

otherSide.line: A recruiter reads your resume against one job, fast: 7.4 seconds on the first pass in Ladders’ 2018 eye-tracking study, starting with your current title and company. A resume written for no job in particular doesn’t survive that read.
otherSide.source: Ladders eye-tracking study, 2018, reported by HR Dive

How long do you expect it to take?

No plan that renews every 4 weeks

capabilities._about: What each tool does, from the dated copy in resume-guide.json (bestFor, freeAnswer) and the scorecard segment. Unknown means not on file, never yes.

problems.label: We’re running hiring on spreadsheets and inboxes
problems.why: An applicant tracking system puts every candidate, stage and conversation in one place your whole team can see.

otherSide.line: Your applicant tracking system is also your candidates’ first impression of you. In a CareerBuilder study, 60% of job seekers said they had quit an online application partway through because of its length or complexity. Whatever you choose, keep the application short.
otherSide.source: CareerBuilder candidate study, reported by SHRM

problems.label: We’re buried in applicants
problems.why: A system won’t shrink the pile, but it keeps every applicant in a stage, so the few you’ll hire don’t get lost in it. Of every 1,000 applications, 32 reach a first interview.

otherSide.line: Of every 1,000 applications, 75 are screened, 32 reach a first interview and 5 end in a hire. For everyone else, a fast, clear no is the whole candidate experience, so set it up before the pile arrives.
otherSide.source: Greenhouse, The Hire Standard, fall 2026: 161.8 million applications across 9,473 companies

problems.label: We’re seeing fake or fraudulent candidates
problems.why: Fraud checks belong in the system every application already passes through. Only a system with fraud detection on file can be the pick; the FBI’s red flags are free for everyone.

guidance.text: The FBI’s red flags, as a checklist

otherSide.line: Real candidates go through the checks too. In Greenhouse’s version, candidates confirm who they are through CLEAR, with biometric and government ID verification. Tell candidates before the interview what you check and why.
otherSide.source: Greenhouse, Real Talent product page, February 2026

problems.label: We can’t find people to reach out to
problems.why: This is sourcing, not tracking. There’s no sourcing scoreboard yet, so nothing here is scored.

otherSide.line: People who aren’t looking can tell a mass message from a real one. LinkedIn’s data shows messages sent one at a time get about 15% more responses than messages sent in bulk.
otherSide.source: LinkedIn Talent Solutions, InMail response data

problems.label: Our interviews are inconsistent
problems.why: Consistency comes from structure first: the same questions, scored the same way. A notes tool helps once the structure exists.

guidance.text: Build a structured interview scorecard, free

otherSide.line: Structure is the best-supported fix in hiring research. A 2022 re-analysis of selection research ranked structured interviews, the same questions scored the same way, first among common hiring methods for predicting job performance.
otherSide.source: Sackett, P. R., Zhang, C., Berry, C. M., and Lievens, F. (2022). Journal of Applied Psychology, 107(11), 2040-2068

problems.label: Our team needs better recruiting skills
problems.why: Software won’t train a team. Training will.

otherSide.line: Candidates judge the company by the person interviewing them. In LinkedIn’s candidate research, 83% of candidates said a negative interview experience can change their mind about a role or company they once liked.
otherSide.source: LinkedIn Talent Solutions, candidate experience research

segments._about: From the ATS guide’s methodology: hires per year decides the tier, because hiring volume is what decides tool fit.

small.label: Small teams: under 20 hires a year, no full-time recruiter

growing.label: Growing teams: 20 to 50 hires a year, a first dedicated recruiter

scaling.label: Scaling teams: 50+ hires a year, a dedicated TA function

mustHaves.label: A price we can see without a sales call
A free plan to start on

fallback.text: Tell us how you hire and get a stack recommendation, free

prices._about: Each system’s cheapest published plan, from its pricing page as quoted in the ATS scorecard (as of 2026-08-22). per: user-month, month or year. maxEmployees: the company size the published price covers; above it, treat the price as a quote. Quote-only systems have no amount. Prices in another currency are never converted.

capabilities._about: What a system does, from its own published product page, dated. Unknown means not on file, never yes. These are features the vendors describe; we haven’t tested how well they work.

Greenhouse.what: Fraud and spam detection, plus identity verification through CLEAR (biometric and government ID)

Ashby.what: Fraud detection built in: flags location mismatches, identity verification issues and technical assessment anomalies

Greenhouse.what: AI-assisted Talent Matching against recruiter-defined, weighted calibrations, without automating the decision

situations._about: Common situations with their own permanent page under /what-should-i-use/[slug], so the answers can be found, linked and quoted. Titles are the question people actually ask. The answer is computed from the data, never written by hand.
